title: AI Strategies and the Informal Economy: Africa’s Job Creation Test
gist: CSIS and the Global Center on AI Governance argue that Africa — adding 700 million workers by 2050 and needing 15 million new jobs a year, with 81 percent of jobs informal — has built national AI strategies in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa that are almost entirely supply-side (skills, data centers, R&D, startups) and contain no concrete measures to reach the informal majority. With informality at 93 percent in Nigeria, 84 percent in Kenya and 21 percent in South Africa, the AfDB's projection that AI drives nearly a fifth of Africa's GDP growth and up to 40 million jobs by 2035 hinges on offline-capable, voice-first, multilingual tools and complementary applications like alternative-data credit, crop diagnostics and freight matching.

insights.claim: Africa is projected to add 700 million workers by 2050, accounting for 85 percent of global workforce growth, and needs to create an additional 15 million jobs per year just to keep pace with its rising workforce.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The single largest labor-supply event of the century — sets the denominator against which every African AI or industrial policy should be judged.
insights.locator: AI is arriving at a critical time

insights.claim: Approximately 81 percent of jobs across the African continent are informal, which limits decent livelihoods, job security and upskilling opportunities, particularly for youth.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Any AI monetization thesis built on formal-sector enterprise adoption addresses less than a fifth of African employment.
insights.locator: AI is arriving at a critical time

insights.claim: Informal employment shares diverge sharply across the three largest economies studied: 93 percent in Nigeria, 84 percent in Kenya and only 21 percent in South Africa.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Country selection matters enormously for AI-adoption TAM in Africa — South Africa is a formal-sector market, Nigeria and Kenya are not.
insights.locator: A Closer Look at Informality in Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa

insights.claim: Informal employment in Kenya and Nigeria is concentrated in agriculture followed by trade and commerce, while South Africa's smaller informal workforce concentrates in small-scale retail, street and market vending, artisanal manufacturing, domestic work and childcare.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Sector composition tells you which AI verticals — agritech versus retail/logistics — actually map to each country's informal labor base.
insights.locator: In both Kenya and Nigeria, the concentration of informal employment

insights.claim: The African Development Bank estimates AI could account for nearly one-fifth of Africa's total GDP growth by 2035, creating up to 40 million jobs across agriculture, healthcare, retail, finance and manufacturing.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The headline bull case for African AI — worth tracking against actual informal-sector adoption, which the piece argues is the binding condition.
insights.locator: The African Development Bank estimates

insights.claim: Because AI productivity gains are currently concentrated in desk-based professional roles, Africa's informal sectors are buffered from near-term AI job losses but at medium- and long-term risk of realizing only limited gains or missing the AI revolution entirely.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The inverse of the developed-market AI story: low automation exposure and low capture potential are the same structural fact.
insights.locator: This job creation deficit is compounded

insights.claim: Projected digital and AI jobs in Africa are gig-based roles that could absorb informal workers only if the right infrastructure and training ecosystems are put in place first.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Gig platforms are the likely absorption channel — connectivity and training buildout are the leading indicators for that thesis.
insights.locator: Projected digital and AI jobs are gig-based roles

insights.claim: Public and policymaker perceptions of AI across Africa are positive, and in a recent survey half of African respondents were optimistic AI will improve their work opportunities in the short and medium term.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Low political resistance to AI deployment in Africa contrasts with developed-market backlash — a regulatory arbitrage worth noting.
insights.locator: Overall, however, public and policymaker perceptions

insights.claim: Informal workers already deploy AI tools for rote tasks such as simple accounting, branding and social media posts, but this use remains relatively limited compared to applications in other sectors because informal work is manual, service- and trade-based.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Current informal-sector AI use is bolt-on back-office, not core operations — the addressable gap for product design.
insights.locator: Given the manual-, service-, and trade-based focus

themes.theme: National AI Strategies: Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa

insights.claim: Between 2023 and 2025 Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa rose 33, 31 and 12 places respectively on the Oxford Government AI Readiness Index, evidencing genuine state-level commitment across AI research, capacity building and compute infrastructure.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Fast readiness improvement is a tailwind for compute, connectivity and data-center exposure in these three markets.
insights.locator: Identifying Focus Areas and Gaps in National AI Strategies

insights.claim: Nigeria's flagship 3 Million Technical Talent program aims to train 3 million Nigerians in core digital skills including AI and has enrolled over 135,000 participants so far, supplemented by a Microsoft partnership to train 1 million Nigerians in AI skills.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: 135,000 against a 3 million target is a 4.5 percent execution rate — the gap between announced and delivered African AI skilling.
insights.locator: For instance, the Nigerian government has largely focused

insights.claim: Nigeria has repurposed its National Centre for AI and Robotics to conduct modern large language model research and partnered with the UNDP to establish regional AI clusters in six universities.
insights.speaker: CSIS
entities: National Centre for AI and Robotics
insights.so_what: State-backed sovereign LLM research is spreading to mid-income markets — a demand source for compute and a channel for local-language model development.
insights.locator: Complementing these are research and development (R&D) activities

insights.claim: Kenya's five-year AI Strategy carries a $1 billion (KES 152 billion) implementation budget weighted toward connectivity, data centers and innovation hubs, building on Nairobi's roughly 500 startups and its role as a major regional hub for Google and Microsoft.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A concrete $1bn public capex pipeline in East African digital infrastructure — the most directly investable number in the piece.
insights.locator: Kenya’s strategy focuses heavily on infrastructure investment

insights.claim: The Africa Center of Competence for Digital and Artificial Intelligence Skilling, jointly established by Kenya with UNDP and Microsoft, aims to incubate public sector AI innovation, train over 1,000 AI specialists and expand AI literacy in Kenyan schools.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler-plus-multilateral skilling vehicles are the standard market-entry structure in African AI — a pattern to expect from other vendors.
insights.locator: Additionally, Kenya has made strides to prioritize upskilling

insights.claim: South Africa's National AI Policy framework draft names 'AI for Inclusive Growth and Job Creation' as one of six strategic pillars, but implementation remains in the balance following the framework's recent recall by the ministry.
insights.speaker: CSIS
entities: Department of Communications and Digital Technologies
insights.so_what: A live policy-execution risk in Africa's most formalized economy — the recall is the specific event to monitor for South African AI investment timing.
insights.locator: South Africa’s National AI Policy framework draft

insights.claim: South Africa's Department of Communications and Digital Technologies is funding the AI Institute of South Africa, which hosts university hubs driving localized AI projects and workforce reskilling in mining, agriculture and government administration.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Mining-sector AI reskilling in South Africa is a specific, fundable vertical with existing institutional backing.
insights.locator: the Department of Communications and Digital Technologies is funding

insights.claim: Across all three countries the AI strategies commit clearly to supply-side policies — skills investment, local infrastructure and partnerships with private technology companies — while lacking concrete policies or measures to spur AI integration in the informal sector.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The central critique: in Nigeria and Kenya an industry-focused AI policy serves only a small fraction of actual economic activity, capping realized returns on public AI spend.
insights.quote: an overtly industry-focused AI policy implementation will serve only a limited proportion of the economy
insights.locator: For all their strengths, however, these three countries’ AI strategies

insights.claim: AI tools that take African informal-sector barriers seriously would need to be offline-capable, offer voice- and image-first interfaces, and work across multiple local languages.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A concrete product spec for anyone building for frontier markets — on-device inference and multilingual voice are the gating capabilities, not model quality.
insights.locator: First, an informally focused AI policy

insights.claim: Because AI has limited immediate utility for direct informal labor such as artisanal furniture manufacturing, smallholder farming or truck driving, the genuinely useful applications are complementary business-enabling ones: alternative-data credit, crop diagnostics and freight matching.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Names the three most investable informal-economy AI verticals in Africa — fintech credit scoring, agritech diagnostics and logistics matching.
insights.locator: Second, implementation road maps to meet policy goals

insights.claim: Closing the demand-side deficit requires resources flowing to informal operators via subsidies, tax incentives and grants, combined with SME support, new forms of credit and blended finance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Blended-finance vehicles targeting informal-sector AI adoption are the likely funding instrument — a channel for DFI and impact capital deployment.
insights.locator: Third, resources would flow to informal operators

insights.claim: National statistics agencies should embed AI-adoption and labor-transition questions into surveys they already run, and combine that public data with privately compiled workforce data for more real-time, actionable insight.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: There is currently no measurement infrastructure for African informal AI adoption — meaning claimed job-creation outcomes cannot be verified.
insights.locator: Fourth, labor and economic data needs to include questions

insights.claim: Cross-border intra-African trade is estimated at only 7 to 16 percent of all trade flows, so making credit, payments and data tools flow seamlessly across borders — under interoperable data governance regimes — is a prerequisite for inclusive AI-enabled economic engagement.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Fragmented cross-border rails cap the scalability of any African fintech or AI-services platform — regional interoperability is the unlock to watch.
insights.locator: Fifth, underpinning all of this must be data governance regimes

themes.theme: No New Strategy Needed — Implementation Choices

insights.claim: The pivots proposed require no new strategies or frameworks because existing policies already contain the hooks: Kenya's strategy names micro and small enterprises as a priority sector aligned with the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda, Nigeria could add an informal training track to 3MTT, and South Africa already has an inclusive-growth AI pillar.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Low-cost, fast-implementable policy changes — meaning the informal-sector pivot could happen without a legislative cycle, making it a near-term catalyst.
insights.locator: None of these pivots requires new strategies

insights.claim: The author's framing is that informality is the test of whether AI creates broad-based work in Africa or simply deepens an existing divide, with a meaningful pathway requiring that traders, farmers, drivers and artisans currently excluded from the AI trajectory be directly targeted.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Sets the metric by which to judge African AI programs: informal-sector reach, not compute installed or specialists trained.
insights.quote: Across Africa, informality is the test of whether AI creates broad-based work that achieves economic development goals and lives up to its promises or simply deepens an existing divide.

insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A forthcoming report with sector-by-sector policy alignment data — a scheduled information event for anyone tracking African AI policy.
